1.title: Project 1 — Financial Research & Analysis Agent [pattern: AGENT]
1.text:
What it does: Give it a company or a question (“Summarize NVIDIA's latest 10-Q and flag risk-section changes vs the prior quarter”). It plans, pulls the filings, runs calculations, retrieves relevant sections, and produces a cited analyst-style memo. It takes real actions across tools — it doesn't just chat.
Why it's golden: Agents that take actions are the highest-demand, least-solved pattern of 2026. Finance is a top enterprise FDE vertical and forces real rigor (numbers must be right, sources must be cited).
Data / sources: SEC EDGAR (free filings API), a market-data API (e.g. yfinance), and the filing text itself as the retrieval corpus.
Tools the agent gets: search_filings, get_financials(ticker), calculate(expression), retrieve_section(query), compare_periods(a,b), write_memo(sections, citations).
Must do: Multi-step planning; cite every claim to a source; refuse/flag when data is missing rather than inventing it; show its reasoning trace.
Evaluation (the point): A gold set of ~50 questions with known answers. Measure factual accuracy, citation precision (are cited sources actually relevant), calculation correctness, and cost + latency per query. Report where it still fails.
Stack: Python, FastAPI, Postgres + pgvector, Anthropic API (tool use), Instructor, SEC EDGAR API, yfinance, Langfuse, Streamlit demo.
Interview probes to prepare for: How do you stop it inventing a number? What happens when a filing format changes? How would this scale to 500 tickers a day?

2.title: Project 2 — Medical-Literature Question Answering [pattern: RAG]
2.text:
What it does: Answers clinical questions grounded strictly in a medical-literature corpus, with citations to the exact source passages, and refuses to answer beyond what the evidence supports.
Why it's golden: A plausible-sounding RAG demo is table stakes; a measured one signals seniority. Healthcare makes faithfulness (no hallucinated claims) genuinely matter, which forces the rigor interviewers look for.
Data / sources: PubMed abstracts (free via NCBI E-utilities) or the PubMedQA dataset (which comes with questions + answers — a partial free gold set).
Must do: Hybrid retrieval (keyword + vector) + reranking; every claim cited to a passage; an explicit “insufficient evidence” path; no unsupported statements.
Evaluation (the point): Using PubMedQA or your own 50–100 Q&A gold set, measure faithfulness (are claims supported by retrieved text?), answer relevance, and retrieval recall@k. Show before/after adding the reranker and the hallucination guard.
Stack: Python, FastAPI, Postgres + pgvector, an embedding model + cross-encoder reranker, Anthropic API, RAGAS for eval, Streamlit demo.
Interview probes: How do you know it isn't hallucinating? What's your faithfulness number and how did you measure it? When would you NOT use RAG here?

3.title: Project 3 — Legal Clause Classifier [pattern: FINE-TUNING]
3.text:
What it does: Classifies contract clauses into types (indemnification, termination, governing law, etc.) with a small fine-tuned model served behind an API, falling back to a larger model when unsure.
Why it's golden: The signal isn't that you CAN fine-tune — it's the judgment of when you SHOULD. You'll prove a small fine-tuned model beats prompting a big one on this narrow task, on accuracy AND cost, and say clearly when it wouldn't be worth it.
Data / sources: CUAD (Contract Understanding Atticus Dataset — free, real legal annotations, gives you labels).
Must do: Establish a prompt-only baseline FIRST; fine-tune a small model with LoRA; evaluate both on the SAME held-out test set; return confidence and fall back on low confidence.
Evaluation (the point): A comparison table: prompt-only large model vs fine-tuned small model, on accuracy, cost per 1k clauses, and latency. The case study's thesis is the when-to-fine-tune decision, backed by these numbers.
Stack: Python, Unsloth + PEFT/LoRA on free Colab, a small base model (1–3B), FastAPI serving, CUAD, Streamlit demo.
Interview probes: Why fine-tune instead of just prompting? What did it cost vs save? When would you have chosen NOT to fine-tune?

4.title: Project 4 — A Public MCP Server [pattern: MCP]
4.text:
What it does: Exposes a genuinely useful real-world tool to any AI assistant via the Model Context Protocol — the emerging standard for connecting agents to tools. Pick something you'd actually use (e.g. a wrapper over a public API that lacks a server).
Why it's golden: MCP is still rare enough on a resume to be a real edge, and it's central to how Anthropic's own FDEs connect Claude to enterprise systems. It's the cheapest project here for the signal it sends.
Must do: 3–4 well-scoped tools (not 20 thin wrappers); real error handling with messages a model can act on; a deliberate choice of what NOT to expose; tests; a clear README; published to PyPI/npm and listed in an MCP directory.
Evaluation / signal: Fewer, well-designed tools beat many shallow ones. Pair it with a short post explaining one design decision and why — that post demonstrates the exact judgment the role hires for.
Stack: Python or TypeScript MCP SDK, the target API, tests, published package.
Interview probes: Why these tools and not others? How did you handle errors and auth? What would break if an agent called them in the wrong order?
